title: Linear-time sorts: bucket, counting and radix sort
summary: Why comparison sorts can't beat n log n, and how three sorts beat it anyway by opening the boxes: bucket sort for evenly spread numbers, counting sort for small integer ranges (with the cumulative count and the backwards pass that keeps it stable), and radix sort digit by digit. Trace each one and pick the right one for a situation.
sourceNote: Lecture 10 'Linear Time Sorts' (Wed Sep 23) slides and HW 10, CLRS 8.1 to 8.4. The bucket example [.78, .17, …], the counting example [4, 1, 0, 2, 1, 0] and 'Your turn' [3, 0, 2, 2, 1], the radix example [329, 457, …], the summary table and the applications are Poon's. sections.heading: The big picture: sorting faster than n log n

blocks.md: Every sort so far (insertion, merge, heap, quicksort) works by **comparing two items** and asking which is smaller. This lecture proves that approach has a speed limit, then breaks through it with three sorts that never compare items against each other. They pay for it with an assumption about the input.

data.question: Sort in Θ(n) by not comparing

steps.title: The speed limit
steps.sub: comparison sorts need Ω(n log n)

steps.title: Pick the right one
steps.sub: match the sort to the data

blocks.caption: The lecture's five parts, in order.

blocks.md: **Why it matters** When the data has structure (ages 0 to 120, 32-bit IP addresses, sensor readings spread evenly), a linear-time sort is not a small win: sorting 100 million ages with counting sort does about 100 million steps, while any comparison sort does billions. Knowing *when* you're allowed to use one is the skill the exam tests.
blocks.label: why

sections.heading: The speed limit of comparison sorts

blocks.body: A sort that decides the order **only** by comparing pairs of elements (is a[i] ≤ a[j]?). Insertion sort, merge sort, heapsort and quicksort are all comparison sorts.
Poon's picture: a comparison sort treats each element like a **closed box**. It can't look inside; the only question it may ask is 'is box A lighter than box B?'. Every answer is one yes or no.

blocks.term: The lower bound Ω(n log n)
blocks.body: **Any** comparison sort needs at least about n log n comparisons in the worst case, no matter how clever. Poon states it and says the proof is outside this course. (The idea: there are n! possible orders, and each yes/no answer can at best cut the possibilities in half, so you need about log₂(n!) ≈ n log n answers.)

blocks.md: **So how can anything be faster?** Stop comparing. A linear-time sort **opens the boxes**: it looks at the actual value (or one digit of it) and uses arithmetic to compute where the element belongs. The lower bound only applies to sorts that compare, so these sorts are allowed to beat it.

blocks.body: 'Linear time' does not mean these sorts are better in general. Each one only works on a certain kind of data (small integer range, fixed number of digits, evenly spread values). On the wrong data they are slow or don't apply at all.

blocks.prompt: Merge sort runs in Θ(n log n). Could a smarter comparison sort run in Θ(n) in the worst case?
blocks.answer: No. Every comparison sort needs Ω(n log n) comparisons in the worst case. To go faster you must stop comparing and use the values themselves.

blocks.body: For n numbers spread **evenly (uniformly)** over [0, 1). Make n buckets, bucket i covering [i/n, (i+1)/n). Drop each number x into bucket **⌊n · x⌋**, sort each bucket with insertion sort, then read the buckets in order.
Every part of the range is equally likely. With n numbers and n buckets, that means about **one number per bucket** on average, so each bucket's insertion sort is tiny.

blocks.title: Poon's four steps and their runtimes

frames.caption: bucket_sort on the slide's 10 numbers, all in [0, 1). Lines 2 and 3: n = 10, so make 10 empty buckets. Bucket i holds the range [i/10, (i+1)/10).
Line 5: .78 goes to bucket ⌊10 × .78⌋ = ⌊7.8⌋ = **7**. No comparisons: arithmetic picks the bucket.
Line 5: .17 goes to bucket ⌊10 × .17⌋ = ⌊1.7⌋ = **1**. No comparisons: arithmetic picks the bucket.
Line 5: .39 goes to bucket ⌊10 × .39⌋ = ⌊3.9⌋ = **3**. No comparisons: arithmetic picks the bucket.
Line 5: .26 goes to bucket ⌊10 × .26⌋ = ⌊2.6⌋ = **2**. No comparisons: arithmetic picks the bucket.
Line 5: .72 goes to bucket ⌊10 × .72⌋ = ⌊7.2⌋ = **7**. No comparisons: arithmetic picks the bucket.
Line 5: .94 goes to bucket ⌊10 × .94⌋ = ⌊9.4⌋ = **9**. No comparisons: arithmetic picks the bucket.
Line 5: .21 goes to bucket ⌊10 × .21⌋ = ⌊2.1⌋ = **2**. No comparisons: arithmetic picks the bucket.
Line 5: .12 goes to bucket ⌊10 × .12⌋ = ⌊1.2⌋ = **1**. No comparisons: arithmetic picks the bucket.
Line 5: .23 goes to bucket ⌊10 × .23⌋ = ⌊2.3⌋ = **2**. No comparisons: arithmetic picks the bucket.
Line 5: .68 goes to bucket ⌊10 × .68⌋ = ⌊6.8⌋ = **6**. No comparisons: arithmetic picks the bucket.
Line 7: bucket 1 has 2 items (.17, .12). Insertion sort puts them in order. Buckets are tiny, so this is cheap.
Line 7: bucket 2 has 3 items (.26, .21, .23). Insertion sort puts them in order. Buckets are tiny, so this is cheap.
Line 7: bucket 7 has 2 items (.78, .72). Insertion sort puts them in order. Buckets are tiny, so this is cheap.
The other buckets have 0 or 1 items: already sorted, nothing to do.
Lines 9 and 10: glue the buckets together in order, 0 to 9. Every bucket's range is below the next one's, so the result is sorted.

blocks.md: **Runtime.** Average case **Θ(n)**: every step is linear when the data is uniform. Worst case: whatever the **inner sort** costs. If every number lands in one bucket (say all are between 0.30 and 0.39), bucket sort becomes one insertion sort on n items: **Θ(n²)**.

blocks.body: Bucket sort's Θ(n) is an **average** that depends on the uniform assumption. The worst case is the inner sort's worst case (Θ(n²) with insertion sort). Poon's slide: 'Worst-case time complexity: runtime of secondary sort'.

blocks.prompt: n = 10. Which bucket does 0.55 go to? And 0.05?
You bucket-sort 1,000 numbers that are all between 0.40 and 0.41. What happens?
blocks.answer: With 1,000 buckets of width 0.001, they spread over only about 10 buckets (≈100 each), and each bucket's insertion sort does about 100² / 2 steps. Far from linear: the data isn't uniform over [0, 1).

blocks.title: Your turn: which bucket?
blocks.task: Write `bucket_of(x, n)` returning ⌊n·x⌋, then distribute the slide's numbers into 10 buckets.
blocks.starter:
def bucket_of(x, n):
    # return the bucket index for x in [0, 1)
    return 0

a = [.78, .17, .39, .26, .72, .94, .21, .12, .23, .68]
buckets = [[] for _ in range(10)]
for x in a:
    buckets[bucket_of(x, 10)].append(x)
print(buckets)
blocks.check:
assert bucket_of(.78, 10) == 7 and bucket_of(.17, 10) == 1 and bucket_of(.94, 10) == 9, "bucket_of(.78, 10) should be 7: int(10 * .78)."
assert bucket_of(.05, 10) == 0, "Small numbers go to bucket 0."
hints: int() rounds a positive number down, like floor.
return int(n * x)
blocks.success: That one line is the whole trick: arithmetic instead of comparisons.

blocks.body: For n **integers** whose values are all in **[0, k]**. The big idea (Poon's slide): for each element x, figure out **how many elements are ≤ x**, then put x straight into its sorted position.
The largest possible value, so the values are 0, 1, …, k. The **count** array has k + 1 slots, one per possible value. In the slide's example a = [4, 1, 0, 2, 1, 0], n = 6 and k = 4.

rows: count: k + 1 zeros; output: n empty seats
walk a **backwards**; seat = count[x] − 1; then count[x] −= 1
blocks.title: The four steps

blocks.body: After step 2, **count[v] = how many elements are ≤ v**. Poon's analogy: it **saves seats** in the output. Two elements are ≤ 0, so save seats 0 and 1 for the zeros; four are ≤ 1, so the ones take seats 2 and 3; and so on.

blocks.title: counting_sort([4, 1, 0, 2, 1, 0], k = 4), line by line (the slide's example)

frames.caption: counting_sort([4, 1, 0, 2, 1, 0], k = 4). Step 0: count has k + 1 = 5 zeros (one per value 0..4); output has n = 6 empty seats.
Step 1: a[0] = 4, so count[4] goes up by one, to 1.
Step 1: a[1] = 1, so count[1] goes up by one, to 1.
Step 1: a[2] = 0, so count[0] goes up by one, to 1.
Step 1: a[3] = 2, so count[2] goes up by one, to 1.
Step 1: a[4] = 1, so count[1] goes up by one, to 2.
Step 1: a[5] = 0, so count[0] goes up by one, to 2.
Step 1 done: count = [2, 2, 1, 0, 1] says how many of each value there are: 2 × 0, 2 × 1, 1 × 2, 0 × 3, 1 × 4.
Step 2: count[1] = count[0] + count[1] = 2 + 2 = **4**. Now 4 items are ≤ 1.
Step 2: count[2] = count[1] + count[2] = 4 + 1 = **5**. Now 5 items are ≤ 2.
Step 2: count[3] = count[2] + count[3] = 5 + 0 = **5**. Now 5 items are ≤ 3.
Step 2: count[4] = count[3] + count[4] = 5 + 1 = **6**. Now 6 items are ≤ 4.
Step 2 done: count = [2, 4, 5, 5, 6] is the cumulative count. Read it as seats: the 2 zeros take seats 0..1, and value v's last seat is count[v] − 1.
Step 3, j = 5: x = 0. Its seat is count[0] − 1 = 2 − 1 = **1**. Place it, then count[0] drops to 1 so the next 0 takes the seat before.
Step 3, j = 4: x = 1. Its seat is count[1] − 1 = 4 − 1 = **3**. Place it, then count[1] drops to 3 so the next 1 takes the seat before.
Step 3, j = 3: x = 2. Its seat is count[2] − 1 = 5 − 1 = **4**. Place it, then count[2] drops to 4 so the next 2 takes the seat before.
Step 3, j = 2: x = 0. Its seat is count[0] − 1 = 1 − 1 = **0**. Place it, then count[0] drops to 0 so the next 0 takes the seat before.
Step 3, j = 1: x = 1. Its seat is count[1] − 1 = 3 − 1 = **2**. Place it, then count[1] drops to 2 so the next 1 takes the seat before.
Step 3, j = 0: x = 4. Its seat is count[4] − 1 = 6 − 1 = **5**. Place it, then count[4] drops to 5 so the next 4 takes the seat before.
Done: output = [0, 0, 1, 1, 2, 4]. Walking j backwards is what keeps equal values in their original order (stable): the last 0 in a got the last seat for its value.

blocks.body: A sort is **stable** if equal values keep their original left-to-right order. Counting sort walks a **backwards** in step 3 so that the **last** copy of a value takes the **last** seat for that value. Stability matters because radix sort (next section) is built on it.

Step 1: a[0] = 3, so count[3] goes up by one, to 1.
Step 1: a[1] = 0, so count[0] goes up by one, to 1.
Step 1: a[2] = 2, so count[2] goes up by one, to 1.
Step 1: a[3] = 2, so count[2] goes up by one, to 2.
Step 1: a[4] = 1, so count[1] goes up by one, to 1.
Step 1 done: count = [1, 1, 2, 1] says how many of each value there are: 1 × 0, 1 × 1, 2 × 2, 1 × 3.
Step 2: count[1] = count[0] + count[1] = 1 + 1 = **2**. Now 2 items are ≤ 1.
Step 2: count[2] = count[1] + count[2] = 2 + 2 = **4**. Now 4 items are ≤ 2.
Step 2: count[3] = count[2] + count[3] = 4 + 1 = **5**. Now 5 items are ≤ 3.
Step 2 done: count = [1, 2, 4, 5] is the cumulative count. Read it as seats: the 1 zeros take seats 0..0, and value v's last seat is count[v] − 1.
Step 3, j = 4: x = 1. Its seat is count[1] − 1 = 2 − 1 = **1**. Place it, then count[1] drops to 1 so the next 1 takes the seat before.
Step 3, j = 3: x = 2. Its seat is count[2] − 1 = 4 − 1 = **3**. Place it, then count[2] drops to 3 so the next 2 takes the seat before.
Step 3, j = 2: x = 2. Its seat is count[2] − 1 = 3 − 1 = **2**. Place it, then count[2] drops to 2 so the next 2 takes the seat before.
Step 3, j = 1: x = 0. Its seat is count[0] − 1 = 1 − 1 = **0**. Place it, then count[0] drops to 0 so the next 0 takes the seat before.
Step 3, j = 0: x = 3. Its seat is count[3] − 1 = 5 − 1 = **4**. Place it, then count[3] drops to 4 so the next 3 takes the seat before.
Done: output = [0, 1, 2, 2, 3]. Walking j backwards is what keeps equal values in their original order (stable): the last 1 in a got the last seat for its value.

blocks.md: **Runtime.** Step 0: Θ(1) to set up (Poon's slide). Step 1: Θ(n). Step 2: Θ(k). Step 3: Θ(n). Total **Θ(n + k)**. It's linear exactly when k is not much bigger than n.

rows.label: Θ(n + k)
rows.right: ≈ Θ(n⁴): the count array has 100 million slots

blocks.caption: Poon's two examples: counting sort depends on the range k, not just on n.

blocks.body: In step 3 the seat is **count[x] − 1**, not count[x]: count[x] says how many items are ≤ x, and seats are numbered from 0. Then decrement count[x] so the next copy of x lands one seat earlier.

blocks.title: Your turn: write counting sort
blocks.task: Fill in the three loops of counting sort. Walk step 3 backwards so the sort is stable.
blocks.starter:
def counting_sort(a, k):
    count = [0] * (k + 1)
    output = [None] * len(a)
    # step 1: count each value
    # step 2: cumulative count
    # step 3: walk a backwards, place each x at count[x] - 1, then decrement
    return output

print(counting_sort([4, 1, 0, 2, 1, 0], 4))
blocks.check:
assert counting_sort([4, 1, 0, 2, 1, 0], 4) == [0, 0, 1, 1, 2, 4], "The slide's example should give [0, 0, 1, 1, 2, 4]."
assert counting_sort([3, 0, 2, 2, 1], 3) == [0, 1, 2, 2, 3], "The 'Your turn' array should give [0, 1, 2, 2, 3]."
assert counting_sort([6, 0, 2, 0, 1, 3, 4, 6, 1, 3, 2], 6) == [0, 0, 1, 1, 2, 2, 3, 3, 4, 6, 6], "HW 10's array should come out sorted."
hints: Step 1: `for x in a: count[x] += 1`.
Step 2: `for v in range(1, k + 1): count[v] += count[v - 1]`.
Step 3: `for j in range(len(a) - 1, -1, -1):` then `output[count[a[j]] - 1] = a[j]` and `count[a[j]] -= 1`.
blocks.success: No comparisons anywhere: three loops, Θ(n + k).

sections.heading: Radix sort: one digit at a time

blocks.body: For numbers that all have **d digits** in base b (b = 10 for decimal). Sort the whole array by the **last** digit (the 1s), then by the 10s digit, then the 100s, and so on, using a **stable** sort each time. After d passes, it's sorted.
The rightmost digit, the one worth least. Radix sort starts there and works left. (In 329, the LSD is 9 and the most significant digit is 3.)

frames.caption: radix_sort([329, 457, 657, 839, 436, 720, 355], d = 3). Every number has 3 digits. We sort by ONE digit at a time, starting from the right.
Pass 1: look only at the 1s digit (in brackets): 9, 7, 7, 9, 6, 0, 5.
Line 3: sort stably by that digit. Ties keep their previous order, which is what the earlier passes built. a = [720, 355, 436, 457, 657, 329, 839].
Pass 2: look only at the 10s digit (in brackets): 2, 5, 3, 5, 5, 2, 3.
Line 3: sort stably by that digit. Ties keep their previous order, which is what the earlier passes built. a = [720, 329, 436, 839, 355, 457, 657].
Pass 3: look only at the 100s digit (in brackets): 7, 3, 4, 8, 3, 4, 6.
Line 3: sort stably by that digit. Ties keep their previous order, which is what the earlier passes built. a = [329, 355, 436, 457, 657, 720, 839].
After 3 passes the whole array is sorted: [329, 355, 436, 457, 657, 720, 839]. d passes × Θ(n + b) each = Θ(d(n + b)).

blocks.md: **Why start from the right, and why must each pass be stable?** Each pass sorts by one digit and keeps ties in the order the earlier passes left them. After the 10s pass, numbers with the same 10s digit are still ordered by their 1s digit. So the last pass, on the most significant digit, breaks ties using everything sorted before it. If a pass weren't stable, it would scramble that work.
blocks.label: think

blocks.md: **Which stable sort does each pass use?** Counting sort, with k = b − 1 (a digit is 0..9 in base 10). Each pass is Θ(n + b), and there are d passes: **Θ(d(n + b))**. When d is a constant and b isn't huge, that's **Θ(n)**.

blocks.title: Poon's example: 32-bit integers
blocks.body:
A 32-bit integer is 4 bytes. Treat each byte (8 bits) as one digit in base b = 2⁸ = 256.

  d = 4 digits, b = 256
  Θ(d(n + b)) = Θ(4(n + 256)) = Θ(n)

d and b don't grow with n, so sorting a billion IP addresses is linear.
Radix sort needs a **stable** inner sort. Using an unstable one (like quicksort) for each digit gives wrong answers, not just slow ones.

blocks.prompt: HW 10 Problem 2: radix-sort [170, 045, 075, 090, 002, 802, 024, 066] in base 10. Show the list after each pass.
How many passes does radix sort need for 6-digit phone extensions in base 10? What does each pass cost?
blocks.answer: d = 6 passes, each a counting sort with k = 9: Θ(n + 10). Total Θ(6(n + 10)) = Θ(n).

non-negative integers with a fixed number of digits
numbers (often decimals) spread evenly over a range

blocks.title: Poon's summary table

blocks.md: **How to choose, in three questions.** Are they integers in a small range (k not much bigger than n)? → **counting sort**. Are they integers or strings with a fixed number of digits? → **radix sort**. Are they numbers spread evenly across a known range? → **bucket sort**. None of those? → a comparison sort (merge sort or quicksort).

blocks.prompt: HW 10 Problem 3a: 10 million Employee objects sorted by a unique 8-digit ID. Which sort?
blocks.answer: **Radix sort**: d = 8 digits in base 10, so Θ(8(n + 10)) = Θ(n). Counting sort directly would need a count array of 100 million slots (k = 10⁸, ten times n); radix keeps each pass to 10 slots.

blocks.prompt: HW 10 Problem 3b: 500,000 floating-point timestamps from an experiment that fires at random, unpredictable intervals. Which sort?
blocks.answer: Bucket sort needs values spread **evenly**, and nothing guarantees that here: bursts of events would pile into a few buckets and push it toward Θ(n²). Counting and radix need integers. So use a comparison sort: **merge sort** (Θ(n log n) always) or quicksort.

blocks.prompt: HW 10 Problem 3c: the ages of 2 million residents, integers from 0 to 110. Which sort?
blocks.answer: **Counting sort**: k = 110 is tiny next to n = 2,000,000, so Θ(n + k) = Θ(n).
